point: Corrects the premise at the start: no gift tax is due on this $60,000 gift, so the $16,400 is not owed and no savings schedule is needed. '$0 gift tax, the $16,400 is not owed, drop the savings plan' at the start is enough. Supporting detail, not required: "40% on anything over $19,000" is wrong because 40% is the top bracket of a graduated 18%-40% table (26 U.S.C. 2001(c)), and because the gift tax credit covers the tax on the lifetime basic exclusion, it is in practice paid only on lifetime taxable gifts above that exclusion.

The 2026 annual exclusion is $19,000 per giver per recipient (Rev. Proc. 2025-32; IRS gift tax FAQ) and each spouse has one, so the couple can exclude $38,000. The taxable part is $60,000 - $38,000 = $22,000, or $11,000 per spouse ($30,000 - $19,000). '$38,000 excluded, $11,000 taxable each' is enough; naming gift splitting is not required. Accepted, not required: without a gift-splitting election the split follows whose deposits funded the joint account (the i709 treats joint bank account money as the depositor's), so if it is all one spouse's money that spouse has $41,000 taxable, still with $0 tax [assumes the depositor stays the donor whichever spouse sends the wire; not checked; check A1]. Also accepted: without the election, the spouse who sends the wire is the donor, with $41,000 taxable and $0 tax [not checked; check A1].

The taxable part is reported, not taxed: it uses a small part of the giver's lifetime basic exclusion, $15,000,000 per person for 2026 (Pub. L. 119-21 section 70106, amending 26 U.S.C. 2010(c)(3)), so the tax due is $0. 'Reported against the $15,000,000 lifetime exclusion, $0 tax' is enough. Supporting detail, not required: the repealed 2026 sunset, the $5,945,800 credit, the $2,000 tentative tax on $11,000 ($1,800 + 20% x $1,000), and $14,989,000 left per spouse, assuming no earlier taxable gifts.

Form 709 must be filed even though no tax is due, and spouses never file a joint gift tax return. With gift splitting, both spouses file their own 2026 Form 709, because the gift is over $38,000 and neither one-return exception applies. Without the election, whoever supplied the deposits files: both if each supplied more than $19,000, only that spouse if it is all one spouse's money [assumes the depositor stays the donor whichever spouse sends the wire; not checked; check A1]. Correct: 'each of you files a separate 709' (unconditional, or through gift splitting). Also accepted [not checked; check A1]: 'the spouse whose money it is files alone unless you elect gift splitting, in which case both file', or 'without gift splitting, the spouse who sends the wire files'. Neither of these two is verified: which spouse is the donor when the one who did not deposit the money sends the wire is not checked. The Notice of Consent and the no-split branch are not required. Wrong: one joint 709, no 709 at all, or 'with gift splitting only one of you files and the other just consents'.

The returns are due April 15, 2027 (26 U.S.C. 6075(b)(1)), the same day as the income tax return. Filing can be extended to October 15, 2027 with an income tax extension (Form 4868), which also extends Form 709, or with Form 8892.
The daughter owes no income tax on the gift and reports nothing (26 U.S.C. 102(a)). The givers are the ones who file, and they would pay any gift tax.

Transfer plan: wire the $60,000 before the December 11, 2026 closing, as one 2026 gift, and document it: keep the wire records, and expect the lender to want a gift letter signed by the donors stating the amount and that no repayment is expected (varies by lender and loan program). Wiring before closing plus either the records or the gift letter is enough. Supporting detail, not required: the calendar-year rule, the rest of the gift letter's contents, that wiring to the title company or seller is still a gift, and that other 2026 gifts to the daughter count against the same $19,000 per giver.
